    #99886. Industry News: The Best Places to Go in Australia, Upcoming Zealand, and the South Pacific in 2027

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4111 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: The Best Places to Go in Australia, Upcoming Zealand, and the South Pacific in 2027

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it comes to the best places to go in Australia, Upcoming Zealand, and the South Pacific for 2027, there is a prevailing theme: Familiar destinations are finding new ways to surprise us.
    • This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.
    • Go for: ancient cultural sites, eco-tourism, dazzling island landscapes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it comes to the best places to go in Australia, Upcoming Zealand, and the South Pacific for 2027, there is a prevailing theme: Familiar destinations are finding new ways to surprise us. In Queensland, old pubs have become home to some of the hottest tables. Just take a look at Noosa’s restored 100-year-old Kin Kin, which has a new lease on life thanks to the arrival of Michelin-trained chef Oscar Holgado. And there’s much more where that came from. Across the country in the East Kimberley, this is the year to dine on native bush foods in the shadow of ancient boabs and red cliffs, and rest your head at the area’s stalwart bush lodges, two of which have just reopened after major renovations. Then there’s Tasmania’s east coast, which is always deserving of a long road trip—and now Tasmanian malt whisky is being made in an oyster hatchery, not far from where little penguins (the world’s smallest penguin species) return to shore after feeding at sea. Across the Tasman, Wellington’s new Michelin guide reminds us that even those stars can’t capture the effortless excellence of this area’s food and wine culture. Plan your visit around a culinary festival, several of which come to life in winter, and you’ll see what we mean. Meanwhile, in the Cook Islands at Highland Paradise on Rarotonga, descendants of the original Tinomana community guide visitors through a 600-year-old ancestral mountain settlement, sharing its history and traditions as they optimistically await UNESCO’s answer on recognition. On our below list of the best places to travel in Oceania for 2027, there is a trip for every type. —Chloe Sachdev.

    This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

    Go for: ancient cultural sites, eco-tourism, dazzling island landscapes.

    On the South Pacific, the 15 isles of Cook Islands are scattered across nearly 900,000 square miles.

    Sources indicate that the Cook Islands’ 15 isles stipple roughly 849,000 square miles of the South Pacific, but total less than 100 square miles of land. Most first trips center on a southern pair of islands: Rarotonga and Aitutaki. On the one-hour propeller flight between two, the entire country arrives in flashes: a volcanic ridge inside a white reef, miles of open Pacific, then a blue lagoon with motu gathered along its rim. Rarotonga’s 20-mile coast road threads between reef and pleated peaks, while Aitutaki is defined by its broad lagoon.

    In a recent development, on the west side of the island Rarotonga, a narrow road climbs from the lagoon into Maungaroa Valley, where a canopy of multi-trunked mato trees covers the remains of a centuries-old settlement. Taken together, the surviving sites form a cultural landscape that will appear before UNESCO’s World Heritage Committee in 2027 as the Cook Islands’ first nomination. At Highland Paradise, a cultural site within the old settlement and managed by descendants of Chief Tinomana, the Tapu’ae Day Tour follows those paths past chiefly house sites and sacred ground as guides explain how the stonework organized life here.

    On Aitutaki, customary stewardship extends well below the waterline. In 2025 three lagoon zones came under ra’ui, a traditional temporary closure that allows coral and fish populations to recover, with protections scheduled to rotate in 2027. Aitutaki Coral Restoration takes small groups beyond the usual motu-and-sandbar circuit to its underwater nursery and a planting site, where guests clean a dead coral base and secure a naturally broken fragment. Part of each tour fee supports the restoration work.

    Tourism is growing alongside the conservation push. In March 2027 a new, locally owned hotel, Grand Resort, billing itself as the island’s first five-star hotel, is scheduled to open with 61 adults-only suites on Rarotonga’s west coast. The Destination Stewardship Initiative 2026–2030, meanwhile, shifts the focus from mainly growing tourism to managing its impact with protections for culture and the environment with a greater share flowing to island communities. —Paul Jebara.

    Go for: red dirt, remote lodges, and wilderness on an epic scale.

    After a multimillion-dollar transformation, Bullo River Station will reopen in May 2027.

    Bullo River Station guests will have the opportunity to watch the seasonal mustering of cattle.

    It’s not just helicopter blades creating a hum in Australia’s East Kimberley. A wave of luxury investment is putting this remote frontier on the global-travel radar—without sanding down the wilderness that makes it so worth the journey.

    After devastating cyclone damage, Berkeley River Lodge welcomes guests back to a revived 15-villa hideaway, accessible only by private air charter from Darwin. Individual decks overlook a croc-filled coastline, while open-air en suites allow galaxy gazing from the bathtub. Just across the border in the Northern Territory, Bullo River Station sits on the eastern fringe of the East Kimberley. Come May 2027, it will reopen after a multimillion-dollar transformation, pairing a new level of comfort with conservation across its 400,000 acres. The good news is that it remains a dusty working cattle station: Guests can watch seasonal musters, fish for barramundi in the river, or helicopter to watering holes for swims beneath waterfalls or to Aboriginal rock-art sites.

    There is even more to come. Abercrombie & Kent, in conjunction with the Billingjul Aboriginal Corporation, is developing its first Australian property: an off-grid eco-retreat offering access to the UNESCO World Heritage–listed Purnululu National Park, which contains the Bungle Bungle Range, where countless tiger-striped domes rise from the earth like sculpted beehives. (Originally slated for 2027, the lodge has been delayed, with a newly introduced opening date yet to be announced.).

    Recent findings suggest that connecting much of this wilderness is Kununurra, a proper Outback town on the banks of the Ord River and the main jumping-off point for the Bungle Bungles, Lake Argyle, and the wider East Kimberley. If your itinerary calls for a night in town before heading deeper into the region, don’t waste it: The surrounding Ord River irrigation area is a surprisingly fertile food bowl. The Gourmet Camp Oven Experience puts that produce to work over four courses, cooked by fire in a secret off-grid location outside town, with dinner served beneath the stars and swinging chandeliers illuminating ancient boabs. —Katrina Lodge.

    Go for: heritage buildings, creative energy, and a new wave of boutique stays.

    In Western Australia, Fremantle's distinct creative scene centers on new boutiques, galleries, and stays.

    Poppy Lissiman’s High Street flagship shines among a cluster of indie boutiques and maker pop-ups.

    Sources indicate that in 1987 the America’s Cup turned an unvarnished Western Australia port town into a global stage overnight. Forty years on, Fremantle has forged an identity of its own. Just 12 miles southwest of central Perth, Freo, as it’s known to locals—and Walyalup, as it’s known to the Whadjuk Noongar people—is the significant city’s grittier cousin and the epicenter of one of Australia’s most eclectic creative scenes. This is, after all, fertile ground for Aussie homegrown musicians from Bon Scott to Tame Impala and John Butler. Now, right here at the mouth of the Swan River, a fresh generation of tastemakers are transforming warehouse skeletons and limestone heritage façades into galleries, natural wine bars, and boutique stays.

    Recent findings suggest that the energy will hit fever pitch in November 2027 with the return of the Fremantle Biennale, which will bring immersive art into the city’s forgotten spaces (dates are yet to be revealed, but the 2025 event stretched over two full weeks). It crowns a year-round festival calendar of street performances, exhibitions, and community celebrations steeped in Fremantle’s multicultural roots. On the fashion front, a revitalization of the central piazza—just down the road from Aussie cool girl Poppy Lissiman’s High Street flagship—is helping spotlight indie makers and pop-up retailers. Fremantle’s historic West End has welcomed several hotly anticipated bars from beloved names in Western Australia hospitality, beginning with much-loved merchant Wise Child Wine Store, which expanded its bottle shop in September 2026 to include a 50-seat wine bar. Around the corner, Cafe Music, from the team behind Northbridge institution Wines of While, earned cult status with teaser weekends of mini martinis and vinyl DJs ahead of its permanent 2027 opening. At the heritage-listed P&O Hotel, listening bar and restaurant Ode to Sirens occupies the ground floor, while bartenders at Reuben’s Supper Club have been shaking cocktails since October 2026.

    Sources indicate that the West End’s newest stay follows the same past-meets-present script. The 11-room Owston Hotel (March 2026), inside the former Roma Restaurant, is a modern locanda honoring the Italian families who settled here in the 1950s. Breakfast comes from Common Bakery downstairs; later, slip next door for a pour at Vin Populi. —Jessie Stoelwinder.

    Go for: new sailings, revived resorts, and a quadrennial sporting showcase.

    Traveling by ship to French Polynesia has never been more accessible, thanks to newly introduced yachts and cruises.

    In a recent development, with 118 palm-studded islands and atolls scattered across retina-popping blue waters, French Polynesia hardly needs help making a case for itself. But 2027 brings new ways to explore this far-flung corner of the South Pacific—especially by ship.

    The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection’s French Polynesia sailings debut in December 2026, with 149-suite Evrima cruising the mountainous Society Islands, where volcanic peaks meet reef-ringed lagoons. In February, Windstar adds a second ship to sail these waters year-round, with the newly refurbished Wind Star joining Star Breeze throughout the Society Islands and the low-lying Tuamotus, a scattering of coral atolls and luminous lagoons. In March 2027, Aranui Cruises will launch Aranoa, a 91-cabin hybrid freighter-passenger ship bound for the remote Austral Islands, the Tuamotus, and Pitcairn. Wild, mountainous, and little visited, the Australs offer a different face of French Polynesia from the one seen in postcards showing overwater bungalows.

    Though there are plenty of those accommodations on stilts, if that’s what you’re after, a wave of arrivals on land and lagoon add to the momentum. On mountainous Moorea, Sofitel Kia Ora Moorea Beach Resort has emerged from a major renovation in 2026, with revamped public spaces and refreshed overwater bungalows. In October, Bora Bora’s legendary Bloody Mary’s returned with a new 53-key hotel on Povai Bay and its sandy-floored restaurant restored alongside it. In early 2027, ELYT Charter Tahiti sets sail as a four-bedroom floating villa for private adventures around Bora Bora.

    But 2027’s biggest arrival isn’t a hotel. In July the XVIII Pacific Games—the largest sporting event ever held in French Polynesia—will bring more than 4,500 athletes to Tahiti, Moorea, and Raiatea for 24 sports and more than 350 events. Among the sports is va’a, traditional outrigger canoe racing that is deeply embedded in Polynesian culture, alongside surfing, sailing, and open-water swimming. —Sarah Reid.

    Go for: Southland’s upcoming cultural landmark, wild kiwi, and dark skies.

    Known in Māori as Rakiura, or “glowing skies,” Stewart Island is an International Dark Sky Sanctuary.

    Recent findings suggest that upcoming Zealand doesn’t end at South Island. Farther down the map is Stewart Island, where the roads run out and the forest takes over. Rakiura, its Māori name, means “glowing skies”—fitting for an island that affords fiery sunsets, a visible Milky Way, and appearances of the aurora australis (southern lights) and is an International Dark Sky Sanctuary.

    It has been revealed that for many travelers heading to Fresh Zealand’s deep south, the journey begins in Invercargill, where the Te Unua Museum of Southland will open in 2027, returning a major regional museum to the city for the first time since the Southland Museum and Art Gallery closed in 2018. Telling the stories of Murihiku Southland and its people, its collection includes rich holdings of Māori taoka, archaeology, photography, social history, and artifacts from the Subantarctic Islands.

    In a recent development, across Foveaux Strait, Stewart Island (Rakiura) comes into view. Oban, its only settlement, curls around horseshoe-shaped Halfmoon Bay. Wildlife vastly outnumbers humans here, where fewer than 500 people live. As many as 15,000 southern brown kiwi, or tokoeka, are thought to live on Stewart Island and, unusual for kiwi, can sometimes be spotted foraging in daylight. Just offshore, pest-free Ulva Island (Te Wharawhara) is a sanctuary for native birdlife like native kākā parrots and flightless weka birds.

    Around 85% of the island is protected within Rakiura National Park, a wilderness of native forest, wetlands, dunes, and granite ranges. For a deeper look at its cultural history, take a boat from Oban to remote Oneke, or The Neck, an early Māori settlement and the tūrangawaewae—place of belonging—of Rakiura Māori. The three-hour guided experience begins with a whakatau, a traditional Māori welcome, and a visit to the Oneke whare (Māori meeting house) before guests follow coastal and native-bush trails as guides unpack the area’s Māori and European history, traditional plant use, and conservation. —Louise Goldsbury.

    Go for: lo-fi beach towns, long sweeps of sand, and a fast-evolving food scene.

    Elysium Noosa Resort joins Noosa's ever-improving food scene, serving an Italian-meets-Australian menu of local ingredients.

    Elysium Noosa Resort is one of several upcoming stays on Queensland’s low-rise, low-key Sunshine Coast.

    An hour north of Brisbane, stretching along 62 miles of coastline and backed by rainforest-covered hills and volcanic peaks, Queensland’s Sunshine Coast is the antidote to both Brisbane’s massive-city buzz and the Gold Coast’s five-star flex: lower-rise, lower-key, but home to an increasingly sophisticated run of ambitious openings that is raising its profile at home and abroad.

    In Noosa the newly opened Elysium Noosa Resort has kicked lively Hastings Street up another notch. Cibaria Noosa trattoria, helmed by acclaimed Sydney chef Alessandro Pavoni, raids the Sunshine Coast food bowl for an Italian-meets-Australian menu of Queensland spanner crab risotto, Mooloolaba king prawns sharpened with finger lime, and locally sourced bistecca. Fifteen minutes south in Peregian Beach, two-hatted (”hats” are Australia’s equivalent of Michelin stars) restaurant Bask similarly puts local seafood, meat, and peak-season vegetables front and center.

    Industry observers note that farther south, Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel, which opened in May 2026, has brought the lo-fi coastal town Mooloolaba its first internationally branded resort, with dazzling views and passionfruit-and-melon vodka cocktails at Sully’s Rooftop. On the waterfront at the Mooloolaba Spit, Fish House Steak & Grill jazzes up lobster rolls with a sunshiny yuzu emulsion. The region is serious about beer too: More than 20 independent brewhouses make the Sunshine Coast Australia’s craft-beer capital.

    In a recent development, inland, Casa Renoir, one of Australia’s chicest stays, will be completed in summer 2027 with six solar-powered villas. Limestone, olive trees, faded market finds, and private pools give the place the air of a Puglian masseria. That same connection to the land is shaping the hinterland’s food scene. Ēthos at Alsahwa Estate serves farm-to-table meals inside a barn on a 30-acre regenerative farm, while, in a plot twist for the 112-year-old Kin Kin Hotel, Michelin-trained chef Oscar Holgado, who has worked in the kitchens of Angela Hartnett’s Murano and Marcus Wareing’s The Berkeley, whips up a daily tasting menu—driven by whatever he’s plucked from the garden—in a converted barn called The Woodshed.

    Industry observers note that for all these developments, the Sunshine Coast hasn’t lost its low-key appeal; it has simply acquired better places to sleep, eat, and drink. Luckily, it is becoming considerably easier to reach with growing international connections and a $170 million expansion of Sunshine Coast Airport’s domestic terminal underway and due for completion in 2027. —Ute Junker.

    Go for: Rugby World Cup fever, landmark hotels, and a reinvigorated country escape.

    In 2027, the Men's Rugby World Cup returns to Australia for the first time since 2003, with the final Cup decider taking place in Sydney.

    UNESCO-listed Greater Blue Mountains occupy more than a million acres of eucalyptus forest, sandstone escarpments, and deep-cut canyons.

    Industry observers note that sydney has never struggled for attention, but 2027 is shaping up as a blockbuster year. The momentum began in November 2026, when Powerhouse Parramatta, the largest museum ever built in Fresh South Wales, opened, bringing cultural heft to the city’s west. Also in November, Chanel staged its cruise 2026–2027 collection in Sydney. First shown in Biarritz, the fashion show found a natural second home in a city where salty hair, ocean swims, and year-round resort dressing are not just an aspiration but a way of life.

    It has been revealed that in 2027 sport takes over. The Men’s Rugby World Cup, expanded from 20 to 24 teams, returns to Australia for the first time since 2003, and Sydney lands the sharp end of the tournament. Over six weeks the city will host 13 matches, including major head-to-heads like Australia versus New Zealand, England versus Wales, two quarterfinals, both semifinals, and the bronze final, before 82,000 fans pack Stadium Australia for the final on November 13—the first rugby World Cup decider in Sydney in 24 years.

    Sources indicate that australia’s first Waldorf Astoria opens in early 2027 on Circular Quay, with 220 rooms and serious architectural pedigree along with floor-to-ceiling views of the Opera House and Harbour Bridge. Kengo Kuma & Associates—behind Scotland’s V&A Dundee and Tokyo’s Olympic stadium—has designed a striking glass-fronted tower on the harbor. Inside, Melbourne-born Curtis Stone will lead the hotel’s culinary efforts, opening a bar and a restaurant—his first in Australia, in fact, after graduating from television chef to serious Los Angeles restaurateur with Maude and Gwen.

    Two hours beyond Sydney, the UNESCO-listed Greater Blue Mountains stretch across over a million acres of eucalyptus forest, sandstone escarpments, and deep-cut canyons, promising the perfect side trip. Near Katoomba, the main hub for exploring the Blue Mountains, the historic Lilianfels hotel emerged from a multimillion-dollar overhaul in 2026 as Ardour Lilianfels Blue Mountains, its 89 renovated rooms and suites set on an 1889 country estate that is a well placed base for days on the trails. The bigger arrival comes in 2027, when Emirates’ long-shuttered Wolgan Valley returns from a $35 million-plus overhaul as the world’s first Ritz-Carlton Lodge, with 40 lodges scattered throughout a 7,000-acre conservation reserve roamed by kangaroos and wombats. —Chloe Sachdev.

    Go for: wild beauty and upcoming-wave stays.

    Long-known for its quiet beaches, Bicheno welcomes newly introduced names to the food and drink scene.

    Dolphin Sands is a rural locality in the local government area of Glamorgan–Spring Bay in Tasmania.

    Sources indicate that this area has long been home to one of Australia’s great road trips, a coastline drive linking Hobart with Launceston via Freycinet and the Bay of Fires. It’s a route of contrasts: the Tasman Sea on one side, forested hills on the other, past beaches and granite headlands, and a succession of fishing towns where boats still pull up with the day’s catch. Lately, though, there are more reasons to pull over.

    It has been revealed that bicheno, two to three hours north of Hobart, is a case in point. The former fishing town turned low-key surf haunt remains better known for little penguins and deserted beaches than sceney restaurants, but a clutch of openings is evening the equation. At homegrown Waubs Harbour Distillery, award-winning whisky is made mere feet from the ocean in a converted oyster hatchery, with fireside tastings overlooking the Tasman Sea. Nearby, Le Gulch pours Tasmanian wines against pastel sunsets, while Parisian expat Tristan Punelle’s Le Coq, serving produce-led dishes by candlelight to a mix of both salty-haired locals and vacationers, is a humble ode to French cuisine. And after days spent surfing with dolphins and walking serene shorelines, Selkie Wellness restores balance at its beach-shack-housed massage studio and contrast therapy garden.

    Farther south, beneath the pink-granite peaks of The Hazards, Saffire Freycinet enters a fresh chapter. In December 2026 the landmark wilderness lodge is unveiling The Saffire Jewel, an 8,600-square-foot, three-bedroom villa with a 59-foot-long infinity pool, a Jacuzzi, a private chef, and an excursion guide. Then, over Easter 2027, the Australian Three Peaks Race returns after a 14-year absence. The competition involves teams heading down Tasmania’s east coast in a nonstop combination of offshore sailing and mountain running. Spectators can watch the fleet depart from Beauty Point, catch the runners changing over at Coles Bay before tackling Mount Freycinet, or see the race finish in Hobart. —Alex Mitcheson.

    Go for: independent restaurants, wineries, and creative energy.

    In walkable harbor city Wellington, dining is defined by spots like Graze, Margot, The Ram, and Hillside.

    For the best expression of Newly introduced Zealand (Aotearoa) food, head to Wellington. Seriously. Michelin might have shone an international light on the country’s culinary scene in June 2026 but Wellington has been diligently perfecting its food culture long before the inspectors came to town.

    In a recent development, this compact, walkable harbor city with a strong sense of community has been a go-to weekend escape for eating and drinking at some of the country’s best restaurants, bars, cafés, bakeries, and food festivals. A cohort of passionate chefs and owner-operators embody this sense of independent hospitality, taking advantage of local produce and the area’s abounding cultural diversity. In Wellington, you’ll find the kind of informal dining that the Michelin system often overlooks.

    So how to tap in? At Graze in Kelburn, chef Max Gordy and sommelier Stina Persen serve a daily-changing menu built around Upcoming Zealand–grown produce and sustainably caught seafood. Over in Newtown chef Tom Adam and Juno Miers’s intimate Margot pairs seasonal cooking with an excellent drinks list. Elsewhere, The Ram recasts the Cuba Street pub as a serious food destination, while tiny vegetarian restaurant Hillside follows a low-waste philosophy grounded in local produce. Another to watch is award-winning Rita, which, in early 2027, will relaunch inside its century-old workers’ cottage as Super Rita, a deli and urban pantry showcasing local growers. The waterfront at Oriental Bay gets a new draw in early 2027, when The Pavilion opens its doors as an all-in-one food and wellness destination in a former 1930s bathing pavilion and band rotunda, with an all-day restaurant, a rooftop bar, and a bathhouse with hot pools, a cold plunge, a sauna, and treatments.

    It has been revealed that bringing more of the creative energy Wellington is known for back to its Civic Square, City Gallery Wellington, a significant hub for contemporary art, reopened in October 2026 with a major exhibition by artist Cornelia Parker. Wellington’s city center continues to emerge butterfly-like from a long period of construction, and 2027 is a compelling time to visit, as several major civic buildings reopen to the public. Hot on the heels of the revitalized Te Matapihi ki te Ao Nui Central Library, the 120-year-old, heritage-listed Town Hall opens in February 2027 after more than a decade behind construction fencing, housing a upcoming, world-class National Music Centre. From April 9–11, the restored venue will stage a new production of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Sunset Boulevard, starring Tony-nominated performer Keala Settle. —Johanna Thornton.

    Go for: major resort openings, reimagined experiences, and fresh ways to explore beyond the beach.

    The Whitsundays' reborn Le Méridien Lindeman Island Resort & Spa and Hook Island eco-lodge are much anticipated for 2027.

    According to recent reports, the Great Barrier Reef may be the Whitsundays’ headliner, with Whitehaven Beach its opening act. Now, though, there are fresh perspectives on the beloved archipelago. Explore Whitsunday Island beyond its coral reef by hiking the 20-mile, three-day Ngaro Track, which threads through subtropical forests and coastline. Along the way, you'll learn its stories through Traditional Ngaro Custodians. There’s also a new way to experience the Great Barrier Reef itself. Some 40 nautical miles offshore, at Hardy Reef on the outer Great Barrier Reef, Cruise Whitsundays has reimagined its floating Reefworld pontoon as an overnight-only experience: Sleep beneath the stars in one of 12 new glamping-style Reefbeds, or below the waterline in one of just two Reefsuites, Australia’s first underwater accommodations, offering floor-to-ceiling windows onto the reef and, if you’re lucky, a passing turtle. Next door the newly upgraded Heart Pontoon, a second floating platform, caters to day-trippers.

    But the biggest news for the Whitsundays is the 2027 rebirth of two long-dormant island resorts. The 209-key Le Méridien Lindeman Island Resort & Spa—the brand’s first Australian resort—will bring an Explore Spa and a raft of water sports to Lindeman Island. More remarkable is the revival of Hook Island, which has been without a resort for more than a decade. The Whitsundays’ rugged second-largest island will get a low-impact eco-lodge with 39 cabins, forest pools, and wellness spaces, making the largely undeveloped landscape of lush rainforest, secluded bays, and color-popping coral reefs available to overnight guests once again.

    On the mainland, don’t miss Sollos Estate, Australia’s first agave distillery, which has just opened north of Airlie Beach. The Whitsunday Skyway sightseeing cable car and a upcoming five-star resort in development for Airlie add more reasons to visit this Sunshine State paradise. —Sarah Reid.

    #99885. Breaking: As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in New Zealand Took My Breath Away

    Breaking: As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in New Zealand Took My Breath Away

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, after taking the 17-hour Air Upcoming Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand.
    • Industry observers note that I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown.
    • I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, after taking the 17-hour Air Upcoming Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand. I hopped around the North Island, relishing Auckland’s food scene, checking into the innovative Hotel Britomart, and visiting Wellington’s Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa. But when it came to the South Island, I realized the points of interest are far more spread out, with the massive Southern Alps to navigate through. The island has wide-open roads, but as an American conditioned to driving on the “wrong” side, I didn’t trust myself behind the wheel. So I turned to my favorite solution as a FOMO-fueled traveler who never wants to miss a highlight: scouring the GetYourGuide day-tour offerings to string together my ideal itinerary, a practice I’ve now participated in on all six continents.

    Industry observers note that I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown. And while Upcoming Zealand’s natural beauty and the genuine Kiwi kindness made every experience enjoyable, the highlight was my grand finale: the Milford Sound Business Class small-group tour starting in Queenstown from a local operator called RealNZ. The round-trip 12-hour excursion brings guests in a glass-roof Mercedes Sprinter for stops along the iconic Milford Sound Road, then aboard a Milford Sound cruise through the fjord known as Piopiotahi in the Indigenous Māori language, which some consider to be the eighth wonder of the world.

    Check Availability at Get Your Guide.

    The wide-open views from the Sprinter van.

    I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed. Each of the 14 black leather seats had a gray lambswool blanket, a plush green pillow, and a bottled shot of Manuka ginger Vitamin C boost juice. As a ginger shot addict who’s constantly searching for the best natural pick-me-up around the world, it was love at first sight.

    Sources indicate that the long journey ahead—five hours each way—immediately shrank as our amicable guide provided context about where we were, explaining Milford Sound’s history, ecosystems, and Indigenous Māori connections. When all was quiet in the car, there was Starlink Wi-Fi to keep travelers entertained by their screens. After a quick refresher stop an hour in at the rural settlement of Garston, we reached the lakeside town of Te Anau, where one of its downtown shops served as our business class lounge.

    Here, the coffee order I’d requested at the top of the day was already waiting in a covered reusable mug with my name on it, alongside a plate of pastries. It wasn’t long before we entered Fiordland National Park, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Te Wahipounam. I looked up through the translucent roof as foliage from both sides of the road enveloped our van, winding through the gentle curves.

    Emerging through the Homer Tunnel, the writer stopped for this first glance of Milford Sound.

    Recent findings suggest that soon, the narrow road opened up, and we made our first stop at Eglinton Valley, an expansive glacier-carved flat where expansive fields of golden tussock grass are broken only by striking triangular peaks. Not long after were the aptly named Mirror Lakes, where the Earl Mountains are reflected near-perfectly in the glassy, still water; and Falls Creek, a craggy cascade that unfolds into a teal pond. During our stop at Monkey Creek, we spotted a couple of kea, the world’s only alpine parrots known for their playful behavior. Next, we drove through the Homer Tunnel, traveling less than a mile through the solid rock of Darran Mountain. Fittingly, our guide changed the soundtrack to the Jurassic Park theme as we dramatically emerged into Milford Sound at last.

    According to recent reports, as we descended through the twisty road into the Cleddau Valley, there were gasp-worthy sights at every turn. One minute we were heading toward a daunting granite mountain wall and the next we were looking out to the waters of the sound in the distance. After a quick stop at a bridge to catch a glimpse of Fiordland's highest peak, Mount Tūtuko, in the distance, we arrived at Milford Sound Visitor Terminal to board the MV Sinbad.

    A bridge across the Tūtoko River, which led to a view of Mount Tūtoko.

    The Cleddau Valley, with Milford Sound in the distance.

    According to recent reports, that's when the premium service was cranked up a notch. After I was welcomed with a glass of local Cloudy Bay wine, I was led to my own bean-shaped wooden table with two cushy swivel chairs on one side and a couch on the other, set against expansive windows that stretched overhead for views of the peaks and falls.

    A trio of dishes containing local ingredients, curated by chef Tom Hishon.

    Then came the five-course tasting menu. Already waiting was a seeded sourdough bun with whipped kelp butter, and it was followed by Fiordland wapiti (a local deer) bone broth soup. Next was a trio of artfully plated bite-sized dishes: paua (sea snail) with black garlic, a bite-sized fried ball made of titi (a local seabird), and roe from Mount Cook salmon. The penultimate dish was wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps plus smoked eel. It was all capped off with a “flat white”—an ice cream–topped dessert playing off the popular coffee drink.

    Between dishes, the captain of the MV Sinbad talked us through the highlights of Milford Sound, steering us up close to its plentiful cascades, including Sutherland Falls (1,904 feet tall), Lady Bowen Falls (531 feet), and Stirling Falls (508 feet). When he noted that Niagara Falls is only about 180 feet tall, I thought I misheard and went over to ask. But despite the massiveness of Milford Sound, the falls exuded a calmness that overshadowed their height.

    Recent findings suggest that the area is home to bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins, and humpback whales, and we caught a glimpse of a Latest Zealand fur seal lounging at Seal Rock. Throughout the two-hour cruise, the peaks—some craggy and pointy, others smooth and sloping—were a reassuring constant.

    Recent findings suggest that feeling rejuvenated thanks to both the power of Mother Nature’s beauty and the gourmet dining, we eventually returned to the van, where a generously sized bag of Marlborough Sea Salt Proper Crisps was waiting on my seat along with a Whittaker’s bar, New Zealand’s most famous chocolate. Of course, since it is business class, I also received a refreshing hand towel as I boarded.

    In a recent development, as we began the journey back to Queenstown, I gazed upward, soaking in the view from the car’s glass roof, with a contented smile. A rest stop later, I was so relaxed that I drifted off into a deep sleep. The next thing I knew, we were back in the city. We had spent 10 hours out of the 12-hour trip inside the van, but I hardly realized it thanks to all the luxurious touches at every turn. In this case, the journey was absolutely part of the destination.

    The Milford Sound Business Class tour introduced in October 2025 as a joint operation between RealNZ and Altitude Tours. I originally saw the offering on GetYourGuide, my preferred tour booking platform for its flexible cancellation policies, but you can also book directly through the RealNZ website. The excursion starts at $383 per person for the business class tour, but a coach version is also available.

    Recent findings suggest that the tour I took transferred from Queenstown, but RealNZ also offers the trip from Te Anau, as well as a self-drive experience. There’s also the option to book travel back to Queensland via a 45-minute flight in a fixed-wing aircraft for an additional cost, though it’s weather-dependent. For those seeking deeper immersion, there’s also an overnight cruise through Milford Sound, with the choice of private cabins with en suite bathrooms or shared bunk-style compartments.

    White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, eric Ueland, No.
    • President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.
    • In a recent development, the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

    In a recent development, the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

    The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

    The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO remarked Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

    White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

    Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

    “It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," stated Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

    "Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray noted in a statement.

    It has been revealed that sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

    Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

    “All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters noted.

    In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

    Recent findings suggest that "I'm not a fan," noted retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

    It has been revealed that "To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis mentioned. "Both are bad.".

    While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he noted the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

    And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman noted in a statement.

    Industry observers note that ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

    An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

    Industry observers note that he served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

    Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

    Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

    In a recent development, ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

    Sources indicate that former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

    David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

    Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

    When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

    Sources indicate that before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

    DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

    #99881. The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With New 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1714 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With New 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them.
    • So who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the new 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one?
    • The scale of the commitment is hard to ignore.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them. The 777-9 is meant to be the jet that carries the world's biggest long-haul airlines through the 2030s, but the program is about seven years behind its original 2020 service date, and the biggest customer has already turned away its first batch. For an industry that aims fleets decades ahead, that is a very awkward way to start a newly introduced era.

    So who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the new 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one? The answers involve Emirates, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines, and Lufthansa, plus a rival Airbus that has already started delivering.

    The scale of the commitment is hard to ignore. According to an order book compiled by Airways Magazine at the end of May 2026, the 777X program stood at 619 orders: 521 777-9s, 63 777-8 freighters, and 35 passenger 777-8s, all of them for Emirates. That is a remarkable number for an aircraft that has not carried a single paying passenger, and it makes the 777X Boeing's most crucial widebody bet of the decade. Airways also noted that the problem is certification, not demand, which is a rare thing to say about a program this delayed.

    Emirates dominates the list. As reported by Emirates itself, its November 2025 Dubai Airshow deal added 65 more 777-9s, worth $38 billion at list prices, and lifted its total to 270 777Xs. The airline also holds options to convert part of that order into the 777-8 or the proposed, larger 777-10. Airways lists the split as 235 777-9s and 35 777-8s, so the exact mix is still fluid. Qatar Airways is second with 124 aircraft, made up of 90 777-9s and 34 777-8 freighters, followed by Cathay Pacific with 35 and Singapore Airlines with 31.

    Industry observers note that british Airways and its parent IAG have 24, Lufthansa Group has 27 (20 passenger jets and seven freighters), Korean Air has 20, and ANA has 20, including two freighters. Air India, Etihad, and Ethiopian Airlines hold 10, 10, and 8. But a long list of customers only tells us who wants the jet. It states nothing about what each of them plans to retire in exchange, or how long they will have to keep the old aircraft flying while they wait.

    Industry observers note that for most buyers, the answer is the Boeing 777-300ER, the best-selling long-haul widebody of its generation. Emirates alone flies 119 of them, plus 10 777-200LRs, according to its own fleet table. As noted by Simple Flying, the 777X is also pitched as a successor to high-capacity four-engine jets such as the Boeing 747 and the Airbus A380, which burn far more fuel and cost more to maintain.

    It has been revealed that the upcoming jet's biggest selling point is efficiency. According to Simple Flying's analysis of range and capacity, the 777-9 seats around 426 passengers against roughly 396 on a 777-300ER, while keeping a nearly identical range. The GE9X engines are expected to deliver up to 10% better fuel efficiency than the GE90-115B engines on the older jet.

    The wing is the other trick: it spans 235 feet, 5 inches (71.8 meters) in flight, but its tips fold to 212 feet, 9 inches (64.9 meters) on the ground so it still fits standard gates. Boeing's pitch to airlines is simple: keep the long range, burn less fuel, and spend less on maintenance than the aging jets on the ramp.

    Boeing 777-300ER vs. 777-9: the swap in numbers.

    7,370 nautical miles (13,649 km).

    7,285 nautical miles (13,492 km).

    242 feet, 4 inches (73.9 meters).

    251 feet, 9 inches (76.7 meters).

    GE9X (up to 10% better efficiency).

    According to recent reports, on paper, that is a clean trade: more seats, similar range, lower fuel burn. The uncomfortable detail is that the older jets have to keep flying while the replacement is late, and that raises a very practical question about timing. Airways Magazine points out that carriers waiting on the 777-9 have had to stretch the lives of older 777-300ERs, A380s, and 747-400s, which adds maintenance, fuel, and cabin-product pressure with every extra year.

    Lufthansa will be the first, with Boeing targeting a 2027 delivery. Emirates said in November 2025 that it expects its first 777-9 from the second quarter of 2027, and its Boeing deliveries stretch all the way to 2038. That means the airline will be swapping 777-300ERs for 777-9s for more than a decade, which is exactly why this story belongs to the 2030s rather than to next year. Emirates still flies 116 Airbus A380s as well, so the transition will be gradual rather than a clean break.

    Others will wait longer. According to Simple Flying, citing the Mainly Miles blog, Singapore Airlines' fleet blueprint demonstrates no 777-9 deliveries in the 12 months to March 31, 2027, with Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Lufthansa ahead in the queue. That timing matters because Singapore Airlines is also planning a new premium economy product around the aircraft, making the 777-9 part of a future cabin strategy as well as a fleet replacement program.

    Even the schedule itself is soft. Airways Magazine reported that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford signaled the 777X would follow the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 into 2027 for certification. So queue position is one thing, but the airlines cannot simply take delivery because they are next in line. The more awkward problem is already sitting on Boeing's property: aircraft built years ago for customers that may no longer want them.

    According to recent reports, between 2019 and 2021, Boeing built around 30 777-9s before the program stalled, including aircraft earmarked for Emirates and Lufthansa, according to German aviation outlet aero.de. By the time they could be delivered, they would be about eight years old and technically behind the final production standard. That creates an unusual problem for a brand-newly introduced aircraft: the earliest examples are already old enough to require substantial work before an airline wants them.

    It has been revealed that as reported by Simple Flying, Emirates rejected the first batch built for it because bringing those airframes up to the required standard would take extensive and costly rework. Boeing reportedly dismantled one early Emirates-bound 777-9 after the cost to fix it exceeded its value. Lufthansa has since said, on its second-quarter earnings call, that it will refuse some of its earliest aircraft, with Boeing contributing financially to upgrade the rest.

    Qatar Airways has reportedly signaled that it does not want early-build aircraft either, so Boeing may pool the rejected jets and sell them in bundles. According to aero.de, an unnamed US airline is reportedly interested in 20 early 777-9s, which is striking because no major US carrier has ordered the type at all. A discounted early-build 777-9 could therefore find a upcoming home, but the fact that airlines that ordered the aircraft in the first place are turning some away reveals just how unusual this delay has become.

    It has been revealed that according to Simple Flying, Qatar Airways put the A350-1000 into service in February 2018, the 777-9 first flew in January 2020 and still was not certified at Farnborough 2026, and Airbus has already delivered 114 A350-1000s against 367 firm orders. Boeing, meanwhile, has delivered none of its more than 520 777-9s.

    Recent findings suggest that air Canada is the clearest example. As reported by Business Traveller, the airline ordered eight A350-1000s, with options on eight more, for delivery from the second half of 2030, to modernize a long-haul fleet that includes 19 777-300ERs. Business Traveller calls the A350-1000 a logical replacement for the 777-300ER, and says it brings a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) versus 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) on the 777 family. No North American airline has ordered the 777-9, so for passengers in the US and Canada, the A350-1000 may arrive first.

    In a recent development, still, a head start is not the same as a better fit. The 777-9 carries more passengers, and for airlines that fill every seat, that may be the decisive metric. The A350-1000 offers the established nine-abreast cabin and a substantial operating track record, while Boeing's aircraft offers greater capacity and is aimed squarely at airlines that need to move huge numbers of passengers through constrained hubs. That leaves the 777-9 with a clear market, but a narrower one than the raw order total might suggest.

    The honest answer is volume and density. Emirates and Qatar Airways run some of the busiest trunk routes in the world, and for those carriers, the 777-9's size is a feature rather than a flaw. An A350-1000 cannot match its seat count, and the A380 is out of production, so the 777-9 is effectively the last major twin-engine option left for airlines that need capacity above all else. That is the strongest argument Boeing has, and it is also why the aircraft is best suited to a relatively small group of mega-hub operators.

    Industry observers note that the test comes in the next 18 months. If Lufthansa takes its first jet in 2027 and Emirates follows soon after, the long order book will start to look like a steady delivery stream. If certification slips again, as Airways Magazine warns could compress the entire handover and training timeline, more carriers may do what Air Canada did and look at the A350-1000 instead. The early-build jets will be worth watching too: how many Boeing can remarket, and at what price, will reveal just how costly the delay has been.

    In a recent development, emirates has even signed options to stretch part of its order into the 777-10, a bigger variant Boeing is still studying. That may ultimately be the most revealing sign of all: the airlines that have waited longest for the 777-9 are still thinking about what comes after it. By 2035, the question may no longer be whether the 777-9 replaced the 777-300ER. It may be whether Boeing's biggest twinjet has finally found the narrow but extremely valuable market it was designed for.

    The Right Tote Bag Is the Ultimate Travel Companion—These Are Our Editors’ Favorites

    📅 06 Apr 2020 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option.
    • According to recent reports, though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler.
    • Recent findings suggest that coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option. From early morning flights to daily office commutes, or even a packed Saturday afternoon at the farmers market, our editors are always relying on their favorite tote. The best tote bags hold everything from our laptops, headphones, and water bottles to sleep masks and our most-used beauty products. Whether you reach for a structured leather version to pack your essential items in or an oversized, canvas carryall for a day at the park, the functions of the right tote are infinite.

    According to recent reports, though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler. My favorite tote has been my everyday work bag for years, but it has also accompanied me on countless flights, weekend getaways, and last-minute happy hours. A reliable tote bag really can do it all. Keep reading to discover 15 of our editors' favorite tote bags and why we can’t live without them.

    Recent findings suggest that coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager. Though I still cherish that tiny bag, my most used Coach item is my leather tote. For years, the Nina Tote bag has been my reliable sidekick. I’ve had it for so long that Coach no longer produces it. On the bright side, the Maggie Tote bag is almost identical to mine and is just as practical. I have put my bag through anything and everything over the years, and there is very little wear and tear. The leather is structured and durable, yet flexible enough to fit everything I need without toppling over. With plenty of interior pockets, my necessities all have a place, so I never have to go digging through the bottom of my bag to find the right lip gloss. Not only do I love traveling with this tote, but it’s also my everyday work bag and my go-to for almost every kind of activity.

    I've never really had a work bag that I truly loved until I tried this one from Cuyana. What I appreciate about the System Tote are the additional organizational accessories that you can purchase to add a bit more structure to the interior. Aside from lugging it to and from the office each day, I use this tote as a personal item on the plane and brought it with me on a road trip to Acadia National Park, and have found it to be the ultimate travel companion. The built-in interior pocket is perfect for storing essentials you need to reach easily, like your passport, earbuds, or some petty cash, and since the bag can be snapped closed, you don't have to worry about anything flying out. —Jamie Spain, travel bookings editor.

    This bag is all about the pockets. No tote has ever kept me quite as organized as this one from MZ Wallace, a brand known for its signature quilted bags. It offers six interior pockets, five exterior pockets, and a detachable pouch, offering me a dedicated space for all of my essentials plus a whole lot more. I’m always impressed at how much this thing fits; an umbrella, my 13-inch laptop, a full change of clothes, and my lunch. The Medium Metro tote features ultra-soft shoulder straps, making it a go-to for commutes to the office. My favorite thing about this bag is how lightweight it feels even when full—it never digs into my shoulders or hurts my arms. More features that make this roomy tote a smart choice for travelers: a luggage sleeve, protective feet, and a detachable and adjustable crossbody strap. —Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor.

    Monos’s Metro Tote has been with me longer than most New Yorkers are in relationships. I’ve had this faux-leather cutie for nearly five years now, and it’s traveled with me through new jobs, new apartments, and plenty of new adventures. I actually bring it to work with me every day—the laptop sleeve and spacious interior keep me organized on my way to and from the office. —Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor.

    According to recent reports, I've received so many compliments on this gorgeous structured bag from Cuyana—it's been a great work bag, with plenty of space for my laptop, planner, Kindle, chargers, and other day-to-day essentials. I wasn't sure how well it would function as a personal item as there's not a zipper to fully close the bag, but on a flight to Aruba, I made use of the leather ties to keep items contained, and found it well-sized to slip under the seat in front of me, even with my toiletry bag and a sweatshirt stuffed inside. I'm also a major fan of the snap-to-close key leash, and the interior slips pockets and zipper pocket. —Madison Flager, commerce director.

    It has been revealed that the bag is perfect in the way a red apple sitting on a teacher’s desk is perfect. It’s classic, without ornament, the kind of thing that expresses its utility in its design. It’s both ubiquitous and aspirational, stirring up images of a dreamy East Coast: a white-sand, Nantucket beach; a shabby, wood-planked boathouse on the coast of Maine; a Gothic-inspired Ivy League campus. I've used it as a carry-on item, a beach tote, and as a weekender. Simply having it out on display in your home has the power to imbue your space with a charming, outdoorsy vibe. —Jessica Sulima, commerce writer.

    Baggu’s Nylon shoulder bag is more durable than its canvas tote bags but equally as stylish. It’s slightly slouchy, slightly structured, and comes in the signature Baggu colors and patterns. The adjustable quilted shoulder strap allows for a crossbody fit, a must-have for me when I’m commuting into the office or walking longer distances (nobody needs their laptop sliding off their shoulder onto the sidewalk). The zip closure and interior pockets are handy for organizing miscellaneous goodies and preventing spillage. Plus, the lightweight material can easily be flattened to fit into my suitcase. I find myself continuously reaching for this multipurpose tote on my way to the gym, office, farmers market, and airport. —Hannah Towey, associate editor.

    Sources indicate that just when I think I’ve run out of room, I haven’t. The expandable bottom of this Calpak laptop tote adds an extra four inches, allowing me to add last-minute essentials or souvenirs mid-trip. Like all products in the brand’s Luka collection, it’s made of a lightweight, ultra-soft, puffy exterior that makes carrying its handle easy. The material is also easy to clean—simply wipe away dirt or spills without a worry. Inside, there’s a padded 15" laptop sleeve, multiple side pockets, and a zippered section to keep smaller items organized. Another feature I love: There’s a zippered pocket on the outside that keeps my phone or passport secure, while still being easy to access. It’s a great tote for commuters and thanks to its luggage trolley sleeve, an ideal carry-on bag for travelers. —M.K.

    As a shopping writer who is constantly running between the office, press previews, catch ups with friends and, of course, the airport, I need a bag with space for all the day’s exploits and then some. July’s Juliette Soft Work Tote is my perfect do-it-all companion. It’s beautiful—I’ve received multiple compliments on this bag as I’ve been whizzing around with it, and the divided interior is really clever. There’s a 14" laptop sleeve to keep tech protected—all the more important when you’re headed on a flight— and there’s also a dedicated water bottle holder too. It has a wide bottom so your lunchbox can go inside flat, plus a key leash to stop the rummage for your house keys. Brushed gold hardware and a buttery-soft faux leather exterior mean it looks effortlessly chic at after-work drinks, and when I'm off to the airport, the removable trolley sleeve slides over my suitcase handle so I can breeze through the terminal. It is my favorite desk-to-departure tote bag. —Charley Ward, commerce writer, Condé Nast Traveller UK.

    According to recent reports, my Strathberry Kite is my most-used travel accessory. Not only do I use it for day-to-day tasks, it comes with me on almost every trip (the exception being adventure travel), and most recently carried me through trips to Lisbon and Istanbul, where I spent weekends catching up with friends and sightseeing. It's an ideal size for a laptop, should you wish to take it, but fits in plenty of other necessary items, too (like flip-flops or ballet flats after hours of strolling through cobbled streets). I love the walnut color and the soft, supple leather. I'm sure this will be a favorite of mine for years to come. —Abigail Malbon, global audience development manager.

    Sources indicate that when I first saw Parker Thatch offers its Jack Tote bag in this unique zebra and burgundy color combo, I knew it had to be mine. I never travel without animal print, and there was something about this colorway that felt perfectly understated yet maximalist. I found it online about a year ago, and it sold like hot cakes—and has been (devastatingly) sold out since. I received it as a sweet gift from my partner a few months ago, who had pre-ordered it to arrive right when it was back in stock. I've been using it as my go-to work bag ever since. It has an incredible amount of space and strength to carry all of my everyday essentials and then some—from my laptop and a book to makeup and toiletries. Because of its exterior fabric as hair-on cowhide, she just needs to be shielded from the rain a bit more than your average bag. If the design is calling your name on this bad boy, it’s well worth the splurge. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer.

    I love anything Longchamp, and this gorgeous beach tote from the brand is my cherry on top of any vacation outfit. It’s large enough to hold a full day’s worth of goodies (sunscreen! sweatshirt! beach read!), but fits on the shoulder with ease. Plus, the toggle on the front keeps things contained in the most Longchamp-esque way. —H.C.

    After passing the gauntlet of a last-minute trip to the British Virgin Islands, I always keep the Foldie Travel Bag on me, whether it’s riding in my backpack during my daily commute or stuffed into my suitcase on longer hauls. The front pocket easily held my thick reading list and two Moleskine classic notebooks; the full 40 liters of space in the main compartment (with the expansion unzipped) fit a week’s worth of clothes, chargers for four different devices, and another bag filled with toiletry bottles, plus room to spare for souvenirs. Another perk: the two inner pockets and wet pocket proved useful in sorting out the bag’s increasingly chaotic contents. The luggage sleeve was a relieving bonus that allowed me to transfer the hefty weight of my zealous packing to my suitcase. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations.

    I absolutely love this tote. Whether I’m wearing it to the office or while traveling, it fits everything I need. Plus, it comes with a separate removable pouch that I use even when I’m not wearing the bag. This slouchy bag is super durable and matches any outfit. —Pooja Nayyar, associate social media manager.

    Sentimentality may cloud my vision, for the tote in my possession belongs to my late grandmother. And when I tell you I was complimented frequently for it while in Italy, I mean I felt I needed to use the bag to beat back admirers waxing: “Wow, is Vera Bradley back?”; “Is it reversible?!”; “The textiles are so beautiful.” I often caught myself fantasizing about dumping it upside down to perform a “What’s in my bag” for nobody in particular—so capacious is the tote that I was needlessly carrying multiple novels within and rarely remembered to leave my toiletry kit on the hotel bathroom counter where it belonged. Handy pockets ringing the interior are just icing, and would have kept my passport safely inside had I ever been moved to act on the aforementioned dumping. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    The county unveiled this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The latest lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper noted.

    In a recent development, the airline intends to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    In a recent development, “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov.
    • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
    • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

    Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

    “I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

    “They got to give us an update,” Tillis remarked. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

    Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

    Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

    In a recent development, duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

    The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who noted over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

    The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

    The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

    Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy stated the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

    Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

    “In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand newly introduced architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

    According to recent reports, A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

    On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he remarked included “some other stuff” as well.

    Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

    Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

    The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

    Thune remarked Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the newly introduced request specifically for air traffic control related complications, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

    In a recent development, “I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune stated. “We’ll hear him out.”.

    Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the latest funding request.

    According to recent reports, “So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., noted on the floor.

    Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
