    #99838. The Rise & Fall Of The World’s First Commercial Jetliner

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1460 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Rise & Fall Of The World’s First Commercial Jetliner

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Manufactured from 1949 to 1964, the de Havilland DH.106 Comet was the world's first commercial jet airliner.
    • The jet rose to enormous historical significance for the entire aviation industry and was also the high watermark for British commercial aviation.
    • Sources indicate that the idea for a British jet airliner was born during the Second World War.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Manufactured from 1949 to 1964, the de Havilland DH.106 Comet was the world's first commercial jet airliner. It was powered by four jet engines and included a pressurized cabin. The engines were built into the wing roots, giving it a distinct, aerodynamically sleek appearance.

    The jet rose to enormous historical significance for the entire aviation industry and was also the high watermark for British commercial aviation. Yet the Comet's success was short-lived. Its design made it prone to metal fatigue after repeated pressurization. Two early fatal hull losses permanently damaged its market position.

    Sources indicate that the idea for a British jet airliner was born during the Second World War. The Brabazon Committee recommended developing and producing a pressurized, nonstop transatlantic mail aircraft that could carry a 2,200 lb (1,000 kg) payload. The conventional wisdom at the time was that jet engines were not fuel efficient or reliable enough for transatlantic flight. De Havilland head Sir Geoffrey de Havilland used his influence to propose that there should be a specification for a turbojet-powered design.

    The Brabazon Committee awarded a contract to de Havilland to produce its Type 106, initially considered a small, short-range jet aircraft, while other manufacturers were also commissioned for other designs. The Type 106 featured untested elements and was financially risky, but the British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC) placed an order for 10 aircraft.

    Recent findings suggest that de Havilland put together a design team to create the aircraft, which was led by Ronald Bishop, the brain behind the Mosquito fighter-bomber. The initial concept was for an unconventional tailless design. However, BOAC's demand to increase capacity from 24 to 36 seats forced the designers to opt for something more conventional. The final version was named DH.106 Comet in December 1947. First orders were then completed, with both BOAC and British South American Airways invested. They committed to 14 aircraft, to be delivered by 1952.

    The first Comet prototype was ready in 1949. On its maiden flight, the jet took off from Hatfield Aerodrome and flew for 31 minutes. John "Cats Eyes" Cunningham, a former RAF night-fighter pilot, was at the controls. The second prototype, G-ALZK, was registered in July 1950 and amassed 500 flying hours. Qantas sent its experts to observe its operations.

    The first production aircraft was G-ALYP, nicknamed "Yoke Peter", which first flew on January 9, 1951. The jet completed the world's first jetliner flight with paying passengers. It flew from London to Johannesburg. By September 1952, all the aircraft in BOAC's initial order had arrived. G-ALYZ was the last to be delivered, carrying cargo on South American routes according to simulated passenger schedules. On August 4, 1952, Prince Philip returned from the Helsinki Olympic Games on the aircraft.

    The table below uses BAE Systems data to show the specifications for the Comet 1:.

    4 x De Havilland Ghost 50 engines producing 4,450 lbf each.

    1,300 nautical miles (2,400 km).

    Industry observers note that early Comet operations revealed its viability in commercial operations. It carried 30,000 passengers and was profitable on flights with a load factor as low as 43%. The jet also greatly outperformed its piston-engined rivals. The jet flew 55% faster, and its faster climb rate cut flight time.

    In a recent development, popular Mechanics magazine wrote in 1952 that the Comet was between three and five years ahead of any other proposed jet aircraft. Writer Aubrey Cookman rode the aircraft on a mammoth six-stop trip from London to Johannesburg. "Scheduled eight-mile-a-minute travel in the stratosphere is here. I did it, and from now on so can you," Cookman begins. "Regular airline life insurance was available at the usual rate and I suspect a few snapped it up," they later admitted.

    It has been revealed that the trip took 17 hours and 16 minutes, but was still about twice as fast as contemporary piston aircraft. These multi-stop odysseys were typical in the Comet's first years of operation. In the summer of 1953, eight Comets left London per week, with the destinations being Johannesburg, Tokyo, Singapore and Colombo. The Tokyo flight took 36 hours, with the same trip on BOAC's DC-4M-4 Argonaut taking over 86 hours.

    The table below highlights the fleet sizes of the Comet's most significant operators in the 1960s, using data collected by Simple Flying:.

    According to recent reports, from 1953, several other airlines placed orders for the Comet. Union Aéromaritime de Transport and Air France both ordered three Comet 1As, which had greater fuel capacity. De Havilland also developed the Comet 2, which had better engines and was longer. Air India, British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines, Japan Airlines and more made orders, although Qantas concluded that the Comet wasn't yet ready for its London to Canberra route.

    According to recent reports, across its service, the Comet was involved in 25 hull-loss accidents, 13 of which were fatal, leading to the tragic deaths of 492 people, according to Aviation Safety Network. That is 22% of all airframes built. The first accident came on October 26, 1952. BOAC Flight 115 was attempting to take off from Rome Ciampino G. B. Pastine Airport (CIA) when it failed to get airborne. It ran into rough ground at the end of the airport. Just two passengers suffered minor injuries, but the aircraft never flew again.

    A fresh Canadian Pacific Airlines Comet 1A suffered a similar accident in March 1953, resulting in the deaths of five crew and six passengers. It was the first fatal jetliner crash. The first airborne fatal jetliner crash occurred on May 2, 1953. BOAC Flight 783 crashed in a thunderstorm shortly after takeoff from Calcutta-Dum Dum Airport (CCU). The jet was seen hurtling towards the ground with no wings. All 43 people on board died.

    The following year saw the notorious Comet disasters of 1954. These were BOAC Flight 781 and South African Airways Flight 201. Flight 781 was the most deadly, with the aircraft breaking up in midair 20 minutes after takeoff from Ciampino.

    "The cost of solving the Comet mystery must be reckoned neither in money nor in manpower," remarked British Prime Minister Winston Churchill. The Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough led an investigation into the accidents. Its work showed that cabin pressurization cycles had caused metal fatigue cracks. The stress had been concentrated near windows and hatch corners, as well as around the automatic direction-finding (ADF) antenna cutout. These small areas of fatigue were sufficient to cause the thin-skinned fuselage to fail, leading the aircraft to break up in midair with deadly consequences.

    The findings resulted in the Comet 1 fleet being grounded in 1954. Future Comet iterations, like the Comet 4, had thicker skin, and areas prone to stress were also targeted. De Havilland completed a refit program to strengthen the skin and wing structure of existing aircraft and install rounder windows.

    It has been revealed that the Comet 4 first flew in April 1958, marking the Comet's return to service. Comet 3 customers canceled their orders and switched to the newer iteration, which had improved fuel capacity. BOAC used the jet for regular services from London to New York, completing the trip in an incredibly short six hours and 12 minutes. It was the first jetliner to make a nonstop transatlantic trip. Yetat this time, the Boeing 707 was coming into service, as was the Douglas DC-8. These American aircraft were larger, faster, and had a better range. The days of Britain dominating jet aviation were numbered.

    A Dan-Air Comet (pictured above) performed the final flight of the world's first commercial jet aircraft on November 9, 1980. The British carrier flew nearly 50 Comets, usually acquiring them secondhand during the 1960s and 1970s, with three Comet variants in the fleet. The final flight saw a Comet 4C take off from London Gatwick Airport (LGW). The plane then made a low pass at London Heathrow Airport (LHR) before making another low pass at RAF Brize Norton. The destination honored G-BDIW's former owner, the RAF, where it was registered as XR398.

    Sources indicate that the passengers received certificates showing they had been on the last flight. The jet then traveled on to Germany for preservation at the Flugausstellung Peter Junior museum in Hermeskeil. The service was not the last time that a Comet took to the skies. The UK Ministry of Technology continued to use the jet to research avionics, radar, and radio-based technology. That aircraft, XS235, continued these duties until its final retirement in March 1997. It concluded 45 years of the Comet being seen over skies in Britain and around the world. The plane is now part of the Cold War Jets Collection at Bruntingthorpe Aerodrome in Leicestershire.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1458 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I rapidly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I rapidly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and revealed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically noted, “that means nothing.”.

    So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    Recent findings suggest that airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    According to recent reports, that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    Sources indicate that back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That mentioned, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    In a recent development, even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    In a recent development, inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    In a recent development, as for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Industry observers note that imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    Industry observers note that it’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of upcoming Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    In a recent development, if I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….
